title: Beige Book — January 14, 2026
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2026-01-14 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

Activity grew slightly to modestly in eight of the twelve Districts, was flat in three, and declined modestly in one. Auto sales were flat to down, manufacturing was mixed, and residential real estate and construction softened. Banking conditions were stable or improving, and business outlooks were mildly optimistic. The report was prepared at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond.

Consumer spending

Holiday spending supported consumer demand. Higher-income households drove strength in luxury goods, travel, and experiences, while lower- and moderate-income consumers became more price-sensitive.

Labor markets

Employment was mostly unchanged, with eight Districts reporting no change in hiring. Firms leaned more on temporary workers and hired mainly to fill vacancies. Shortages of skilled labor persisted in engineering, health care, and the trades. Job switching declined and wage growth was moderate. Firms were exploring AI mainly to raise productivity, with employment effects expected later.

Prices

Prices rose at a moderate pace in most Districts. Tariffs were a consistent cost pressure, and some firms began passing those costs on to customers, though retail and restaurant contacts were reluctant to do so. Energy and insurance costs squeezed margins. Firms expect price growth to moderate but stay elevated.

Notable themes

  • Tariffs: a steady source of cost pressure, with partial pass-through starting.
  • K-shaped consumer: higher-income spending strong; lower- and moderate-income shoppers more price-sensitive.
  • AI: used mostly for productivity so far; job effects expected later.
  • Housing: residential real estate and construction softened.
  • Energy and insurance costs: pressuring margins.

District highlights

  • Boston: Slight growth, strength in high-end goods, flat employment.
  • New York: Modest decline, layoffs at major employers, faster but still moderate price increases.
  • Philadelphia: Slight growth rebound; wages lagging prices.
  • Cleveland: Slight growth, though consumer spending fell modestly.
  • Richmond: Modest growth; weaker auto sales and slower residential real estate.
  • Atlanta: Slight growth; weaker commercial real estate.
  • Chicago: Little change; modest manufacturing decline; loosening financial conditions.
  • St. Louis: Modest increase, attributed to the end of the government shutdown and holiday sales.
  • Minneapolis: Flat activity; slight employment decline; manufacturing contraction.
  • Kansas City: Slight growth; weak energy activity.
  • Dallas: Steady activity; rising loan volumes a bright spot.
  • San Francisco: Modest expansion; price increases intensified to moderate.

Read-through for SPY

  • Slow-but-positive growth with stable banks is a supportive, not exciting, backdrop for broad earnings.
  • Tariff and energy/insurance costs squeezing margins is a watch item for consumer-facing sectors, especially where firms hesitate to raise prices.
  • Spending led by higher-income households makes demand more sensitive to stock-market wealth effects.
